note:
Doctor: Thanks for coming in. I see you're a 29-year-old female with sickle cell disease, and you've been having pain. Tell me what's been happening.

Patient: It started about three days ago. It's a deep, aching pain in my lower back and in both thighs, and it's about an eight out of ten. I'm really worried. Is this going to put me in the hospital again? Is it going to get worse? Did I do something to cause it?

Doctor: Those are fair questions, and we'll go through all of them. First, have you had any fever or chills?

Patient: No fever and no chills. I checked my temperature this morning just to be safe.

Doctor: Any chest pain or trouble breathing?

Patient: No chest pain. My breathing feels normal, but should I be worried about my lungs? I read about acute chest syndrome online.

Doctor: Good that you asked. Any headache, weakness on one side, or trouble speaking?

Patient: No headache and no weakness. My speech is fine.

Doctor: And what are you taking right now?

Patient: Hydroxyurea 1000 mg once a day and folic acid 1 mg daily. For the pain I took acetaminophen 500 mg a couple of times, but it barely touched it. Can I take something stronger?

Doctor: Let's look at the numbers first. Your vitals today are temperature 98.4, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. So no fever and your oxygen is good. On exam your lungs are clear, your heart rhythm is regular, your abdomen is soft, and you have tenderness over your lower back and both thighs, but no joint swelling or redness.

Patient: Is that normal for a crisis? Will the pain damage my organs?

Doctor: The blood work we drew when you arrived shows a hemoglobin of 8.1, which is close to your usual baseline, a white count of 11.2, and a platelet count of 380. Nothing there suggests a complication. My impression is an uncomplicated vaso-occlusive pain crisis from your sickle cell disease. It's very unlikely to damage your organs when we treat it early like this.

Doctor: Here is the plan. I'm starting oxycodone 5 mg every 4 hours as needed for severe pain, and I want you to increase your acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 6 hours. I'm also increasing your hydroxyurea from 1000 mg to 1500 mg once a day, since your counts are stable. Drink at least two to three liters of water a day and use warm packs on your back and thighs. I'm ordering a complete blood count, a reticulocyte count, and a comprehensive metabolic panel for next week, and I'll see you back here in one week.

Patient: What if the pain gets worse or I get a fever? Should I come back sooner or go to the emergency room?

Doctor: Go to the emergency room right away for a fever over 101, chest pain, trouble breathing, weakness, or pain that the oxycodone doesn't control. Any other questions?

Patient: No, that helps a lot. Thank you.
summary: A 29-year-old female with sickle cell disease came to clinic with three days of aching lower back and thigh pain rated eight out of ten, with no fever, chills, chest pain, trouble breathing, headache, or weakness. The patient was anxious and asked many questions about hospitalization and organ damage. Vitals were stable with oxygen saturation 98% on room air, the lungs were clear, and hemoglobin was 8.1, close to baseline. The clinician diagnosed an uncomplicated vaso-occlusive pain crisis, started oxycodone, raised acetaminophen, and increased hydroxyurea to 1500 mg once a day. Repeat labs, one-week follow-up, and emergency return precautions were arranged.

soap.assessment: Uncomplicated vaso-occlusive pain crisis from sickle cell disease; no complication suggested by the blood work.

Increase acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 6 hours
Increase hydroxyurea from 1000 mg to 1500 mg once a day; continue folic acid 1 mg daily
Drink at least two to three liters of water a day and use warm packs on the back and thighs
Order complete blood count, reticulocyte count, and comprehensive metabolic panel for next week
Follow up in one week
Go to the emergency room for fever over 101, chest pain, trouble breathing, weakness, or pain not controlled by oxycodone

c/o low back pain x 3 wks, worse x 1 wk. 7/10, worse at night, better w/ movement.
AM stiffness > 60 min.
Denies fever. No eye pain, no photophobia. No bowel sx, no new rash.
PMH: AS dx yrs ago, HLA-B27 +. Otherwise healthy, no other chronic dz.
Home med: naproxen 500 mg BID, not helping.
VS: T 98.2, HR 76, BP 128/80, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA.
Exam: ↓ lumbar flexion (Schober 2 cm), tender SI joints bilat, chest expansion 2 cm.
No peripheral joint swelling, no heel enthesitis, spine nontender to percussion.
Neuro intact, no focal weakness.
Labs: CRP 38, ESR 52, CBC wnl.
MRI SI joints: active sacroiliitis bilat.
Impression: AS flare w/ active sacroiliitis, failed naproxen.
D/c naproxen.
Start indomethacin 50 mg TID w/ food.
PT consult for spine ROM + posture exercises.
Rheum to discuss next-line tx at f/u.
Dispo: d/c tomorrow if pain controlled. F/u rheum clinic 2 wks.

He denied fever, eye pain, photophobia, and bowel symptoms. Exam showed reduced lumbar flexion and bilateral sacroiliac tenderness, CRP was 38 and ESR 52, and MRI showed active bilateral sacroiliitis. Naproxen was stopped and indomethacin was started, with a physical therapy consult and rheumatology follow-up in two weeks.

note:
The patient is a 74-year-old female seen in the transplant nephrology clinic for follow-up of a deceased-donor kidney transplant placed six years ago for diabetic nephropathy. She lives alone, her only family is a daughter who lives out of state, and she has limited social support and no regular help with her medications. She also has T2DM, HTN, and hyperlipidemia, along with osteoarthritis of both knees.

Since her last visit she reports more fatigue but denies fever, chills, dysuria, hematuria, decreased urine output, leg swelling, or pain over the graft. At the start of the visit she said she has been taking tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, and prednisone 5 mg daily exactly as prescribed. When we went through her pill bottles together she corrected this: because her copay for tacrolimus went up this year, she has been taking only the morning 3 mg dose, once daily, for about six weeks to stretch the supply. She has taken the mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone as prescribed. She also admitted to using over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg two to three times a day for knee pain, which she had not mentioned at first. Her other medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, linagliptin 5 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

On examination she looks tired but is in no distress. Blood pressure is 152/88, heart rate 78, and temperature 98.2 F. Lungs are clear, heart rhythm is regular, and there is no peripheral edema. The allograft in the right lower quadrant is nontender without a bruit.

Labs today show creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, up from her baseline of 1.3, eGFR 34, potassium 4.8, bicarbonate 21, glucose 142, hemoglobin 11.9, and A1c 7.9%. The tacrolimus trough is low at 3.8 ng/mL, with a goal of 5 to 8. The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.4 g/g. BK virus PCR is negative. Allograft Doppler ultrasound shows normal resistive indices and no hydronephrosis.

In my assessment, the rise in her creatinine is most likely due to subtherapeutic tacrolimus exposure from cost-related non-adherence together with ibuprofen use. Early acute rejection is still possible and will be evaluated. Her diabetes is fair on linagliptin and her blood pressure is above goal.

Recommendations for today are as follows. She should resume tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily today and not skip doses. Our social worker will meet with her today to start copay assistance and manufacturer assistance applications and to set up a 90-day mail-order supply. She should stop ibuprofen completely; for knee pain she may use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. Because of her blood pressure, amlodipine will be increased from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. She will continue mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, linagliptin, and atorvastatin at the current doses. We are sending donor-specific antibody testing today, and she will repeat creatinine and a tacrolimus trough in one week. If creatinine has not returned to baseline, we will proceed to an allograft biopsy. Because she lives alone, we are giving her a weekly pill organizer, our transplant nurse will call her weekly to confirm she is taking her medications, and with her permission we will include her daughter in these calls. Follow-up in clinic in two weeks.
summary: A 74-year-old female with a kidney transplant, T2DM, and HTN presented for transplant follow-up. She lives alone with limited support, and after initially reporting full adherence she admitted taking tacrolimus only once daily for six weeks because of cost, and using ibuprofen for knee pain. Creatinine was 1.6 mg/dL, up from 1.3, with a tacrolimus trough of 3.8 ng/mL and blood pressure of 152/88; BK virus PCR and graft ultrasound were reassuring. The clinician attributed the creatinine rise to subtherapeutic tacrolimus and ibuprofen, resumed tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily, stopped ibuprofen, and increased amlodipine to 10 mg daily. Social work, weekly nurse calls, repeat labs in one week, possible biopsy, and two-week follow-up were arranged.

note:
Dictating a pulmonology clinic note on a 54-year-old male seen today for a chronic cough of about four months. He describes a dry, tickling cough that is worse at night and when he lies flat, with frequent throat clearing and heartburn after meals. He denies hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, wheezing, or shortness of breath. He is a former smoker, quit twelve years ago, about ten pack-years. Past history is notable for hypertension and GERD. Medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily, which he started about six months ago, and omeprazole 20 mg daily, which he takes only when the heartburn is bad. Correction, he says he takes the omeprazole about three or four days a week, not every day.

Social note, he depends on the county bus and told me the trip here takes about two hours each way, and he has missed his last two follow-up appointments because of transportation. He asked that we get everything done in one visit if possible.

On exam, blood pressure 142/86, correction, 142/88, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 98.1. Lungs are clear with no wheezes or crackles. Oropharynx shows mild cobblestoning, no lymphadenopathy, and no leg edema. A chest X-ray done today was read as normal with no infiltrate or mass. Spirometry done today was normal, FEV1 94 percent of predicted, with an FEV1 to FVC ratio of 0.78.

Impression, chronic cough, most likely ACE-inhibitor-induced cough from lisinopril, with a contribution from reflux and upper airway irritation. Hypertension is above goal today, and GERD is partially treated.

Plan, stop lisinopril and start losartan 50 mg daily for the blood pressure. Take omeprazole 20 mg every day thirty minutes before breakfast, plus reflux precautions with no late meals. Basic metabolic panel in two weeks, to be drawn at the lab near his home so he does not need another trip here. Our social worker will set up his insurance transportation benefit for future visits, and I will follow up by telephone in four weeks. If the cough persists six weeks after stopping lisinopril, I will order a CT of the chest and bring him back, with a ride arranged first.
summary: A 54-year-old male, a former smoker with hypertension and GERD, was seen for four months of dry cough worse at night, with throat clearing and heartburn, and no hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, wheezing, or shortness of breath. Transportation by county bus has caused him to miss two follow-up visits. Lungs were clear, chest X-ray and spirometry were normal, and blood pressure was 142/88. The clinician diagnosed a likely ACE-inhibitor-induced cough from lisinopril with a reflux contribution, stopped lisinopril, started losartan 50 mg daily, and continued omeprazole daily. A basic metabolic panel near home, telephone follow-up in four weeks, and a transportation benefit were arranged.

note:
Geriatrics progress note, hospital day 2. This is a 79-year-old female who was readmitted two days ago with generalized weakness, poor oral intake, and continued weight loss. She was discharged from this hospital about three weeks ago after treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, and she completed her course of antibiotics at home. Since the earlier admission her poor appetite has persisted, she gets full after a few bites, and she says she feels tired and low most days. Her daughter reports she has lost about 5 kg over the past three months without trying. The patient denies dysphagia, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and cough, and she has had no black stools.

Her history includes hypothyroidism and prior pneumonia. She was walking independently with a cane before the first admission but now needs help to get out of a chair. Home medications are levothyroxine 50 mcg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, which she has taken for years without a clear indication.

Overnight there were no events. Vital signs this morning: blood pressure 108/62, heart rate 72, respiratory rate 16, temperature 97.9 F, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Weight is 41 kg. She is thin with temporal wasting and decreased muscle bulk, her mucous membranes are slightly dry, her lungs are clear, and her abdomen is soft and nontender. Grip strength is weak and her gait is slow and unsteady. On screening, she scored positive for low mood. Labs show albumin 2.9 g/dL, hemoglobin 10.8, TSH 2.1, sodium 138, and creatinine 0.8. Chest x-ray this admission shows resolution of the earlier infiltrate.

My assessment is frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from moderate malnutrition after the recent pneumonia, deconditioning, and low mood. Her hypothyroidism appears adequately treated on the current dose given the normal TSH.

For the plan today, I am requesting a dietitian consult with a high-calorie, high-protein diet and oral nutritional supplements twice daily between meals. Start mirtazapine 7.5 mg at bedtime to help appetite and mood. Discontinue omeprazole, as there is no documented indication, and monitor for reflux symptoms. Continue levothyroxine 50 mcg daily. Physical and occupational therapy to evaluate and begin mobility work. Check vitamin B12 level and repeat complete blood count in the morning. We will discuss goals of care with the patient and her daughter, anticipate discharge to short-term rehabilitation in the next few days, and arrange geriatrics clinic follow-up two weeks after discharge.
summary: A 79-year-old female with hypothyroidism was readmitted about three weeks after a pneumonia admission with weakness, poor appetite, low mood, and a 5 kg weight loss over three months, without dysphagia, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or cough. She weighed 41 kg, had temporal wasting, weak grip, and a slow unsteady gait, with albumin 2.9 g/dL and a normal TSH. The assessment was frailty with unintentional weight loss from moderate malnutrition, deconditioning, and low mood. Mirtazapine was started, omeprazole was discontinued, levothyroxine was continued, and dietitian and therapy consults were arranged with goals-of-care discussion and rehabilitation planned.

note:
Dictating a urology clinic note on an 82-year-old male returning for follow-up of benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms. He reports nocturia three times a night, a weak stream, hesitancy, and a sense of incomplete emptying, all slowly worsening over the past year. He denies dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, flank pain, and urinary retention episodes. Past history is notable only for hypertension, which his primary care physician manages. He takes tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily and says it helps only a little.

Blood pressure is 136/78 and heart rate 72. Abdomen is soft with no suprapubic tenderness or distension. Digital rectal exam shows a smooth, symmetric, enlarged prostate, about 50 grams, with no nodules and no tenderness. Urinalysis today is negative for blood, nitrite, and leukocyte esterase. Post-void residual by bladder scan was 90 mL, correction, 80 mL. His IPSS score is 18, which is moderate to severe. PSA from last month was 2.8 ng/mL. Creatinine is 1.0.

Impression is benign prostatic hyperplasia with moderate to severe lower urinary tract symptoms, inadequately controlled on tamsulosin alone, with no retention and no evidence of infection.

Plan is to continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily and add finasteride 5 mg once daily. I counseled him that finasteride takes several months to work and will lower the PSA by about half. He should limit fluids in the evening and rise slowly from sitting to avoid dizziness. Return in three months with a repeat IPSS and post-void residual, sooner if he is unable to urinate.
summary: An 82-year-old male with hypertension returned for follow-up of benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms, including nocturia three times a night, weak stream, hesitancy, and incomplete emptying worsening over a year; he denied dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, flank pain, and retention episodes. Exam showed a smooth enlarged prostate of about 50 grams, urinalysis was negative, post-void residual was 80 mL, and the IPSS score was 18. The clinician diagnosed BPH with moderate to severe symptoms inadequately controlled on tamsulosin alone. Finasteride 5 mg once daily was added to tamsulosin with counseling, and he will return in three months with a repeat IPSS and post-void residual.

note:
Dictation, neurology clinic. Patient is a 62-year-old female referred by her primary care physician for memory complaints. She reports eight to twelve months of forgetting recent conversations, misplacing items, and repeating questions, which her husband has noticed as well. Correction, he noticed it first, about a year ago. She still pays her own bills and manages her medications with a pillbox. She denies getting lost while driving. She also has trouble falling asleep and has taken diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime over the counter for about two years. She denies hallucinations, falls, tremor, headache, and focal weakness. Past history is notable for anxiety, treated with sertraline 50 mg daily, and hyperlipidemia, treated with atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Alcohol use is minimal.

On exam, blood pressure 128/76 and heart rate 70. She is alert, pleasant, and cooperative. Cranial nerves are intact, strength is five out of five throughout, there is no tremor or rigidity, reflexes are symmetric, and gait and tandem walking are normal. MoCA today was 24 out of 30, correction, 23 out of 30, with points lost on delayed recall, visuospatial and executive tasks, and attention. PHQ-9 score is 6, in the mild range. Labs from her primary care physician show vitamin B12 520 pg/mL, TSH 2.2, and a normal comprehensive metabolic panel. MRI of the brain last month shows mild generalized volume loss and a few small vessel changes, with no mass, stroke, or hydrocephalus.

Impression is amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Contributing factors are insomnia and anticholinergic exposure from nightly diphenhydramine. Anxiety is stable. She remains independent in her daily activities, so this does not meet criteria for dementia.

Plan, stop the diphenhydramine today and start melatonin 3 mg at bedtime, with sleep hygiene counseling. Continue sertraline 50 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily at the current doses. Refer for formal neuropsychological testing. I am not starting a cholinesterase inhibitor at this time. Her husband should come to the next visit. Return to clinic in three months for a repeat MoCA.
summary: A 62-year-old female was referred to neurology for eight to twelve months of forgetting recent conversations, misplacing items, and repeating questions, along with trouble falling asleep and nightly over-the-counter diphenhydramine use. She denied hallucinations, falls, tremor, headache, and focal weakness, and the neurologic exam was normal. MoCA was 23 out of 30, B12, TSH, and metabolic panel were normal, and MRI showed mild generalized volume loss with a few small vessel changes. The impression was amnestic mild cognitive impairment with insomnia and anticholinergic exposure as contributors. Diphenhydramine was stopped, melatonin was started, and neuropsychological testing and three-month follow-up were arranged.

No other chronic dz.
Meds: acetaminophen 1000 mg q8h PRN, ibuprofen 400 mg q6h PRN w/ food.

Lap appy incisions c/d/i.

Continue acetaminophen + ibuprofen PRN.

The impression was a stable fracture without compartment syndrome, so the splint was loosened and re-wrapped, analgesics were continued, and orthopedic follow-up was set for one week.

Doctor: Hi, I'm glad you were able to come in. I understand you're a 19-year-old female with ankylosing spondylitis and you're having a bad flare. What's been going on?

Patient: I've had low back pain for about four days. It's mostly down low, in my buttocks and hips, and it's worst at night and in the morning. The stiffness lasts like two hours. I couldn't get in to see my rheumatologist because her office is two hours away and our car broke down. My mom borrowed a car today to bring me here.

Family member: I'm her mother. We've missed her last two appointments because we only have one car and the bus doesn't go that far.

Doctor: I'm sorry, that makes it hard. Let's do what we can today. Any fever or chills?

Patient: No fever and no chills.

Doctor: Any numbness or weakness in your legs, or trouble controlling your bladder or bowels?

Patient: No numbness, no weakness, and my bladder and bowels are fine. No fall or injury either.

Doctor: Your chart says you take a blood thinner. Which one, and what dose?

Patient: It's rivaroxaban, 10 mg once a day. Oh, wait, sorry, I'm thinking of the old bottle. The one I'm taking now says 20 mg once a day with dinner.

Doctor: Thanks for checking. So rivaroxaban 20 mg once a day with dinner, for the clot in your leg?

Patient: Yes, the DVT in my left leg last year.

Doctor: Any bleeding, like black stools, blood in your urine, or nosebleeds? And any calf swelling, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

Patient: No black stools, no blood in my urine, no nosebleeds. No calf swelling, no chest pain, and no trouble breathing.

Doctor: What other medicines do you take?

Patient: Sulfasalazine. My rheumatologist increased it three weeks ago from 500 mg twice a day to 1000 mg twice a day. I also take folic acid 1 mg daily and ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day for low iron. And I've been taking naproxen 220 mg, two tablets twice a day, from the drugstore, because it's the only thing that helps.

Doctor: That's the part I need to change. Naproxen together with rivaroxaban raises your risk of serious bleeding, including stomach bleeding, so I want you to stop the naproxen today.

Patient: But it's the only thing that helps. What am I supposed to take?

Doctor: I'll explain in a moment. Let me tell you what I found. Your temperature is 98.4, heart rate 82, blood pressure 114/70, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Your low back doesn't bend forward as far as it should, and the joints at the base of your spine are tender on both sides. The middle of your spine isn't tender, your leg strength and sensation are normal, and your calves are soft and not swollen. Our blood tests show a hemoglobin of 11.4, which fits your iron deficiency anemia, platelets of 250, and a CRP of 24, which is elevated and matches the inflammation from your ankylosing spondylitis. The X-ray of your lumbar spine and pelvis shows sacroiliitis on both sides and no fracture.

Doctor: My impression is a flare of ankylosing spondylitis with active sacroiliitis, with no sign of a nerve problem, an infection, or a new clot. Here's the plan. Stop the naproxen. Start acetaminophen 1000 mg every 6 hours as needed, no more than 4000 mg in a day, plus heat and gentle stretching. Keep taking rivaroxaban 20 mg once a day, sulfasalazine 1000 mg twice a day, folic acid, and iron. I'll send today's note to your rheumatologist and ask for a telehealth visit this week so you don't need a ride, and they can talk with you about a stronger medicine. Our social worker will give you information on your insurance's free ride benefit for in-person visits. Go to the emergency room for new numbness, weakness, loss of bladder control, black stools or any bleeding, calf swelling, or chest pain.

Patient: A video visit would be a big help. Okay, thank you.

Transportation barriers have caused her to miss two rheumatology visits, and she had been taking over-the-counter naproxen with her anticoagulant. She denied fever, chills, neurologic symptoms, bleeding, and signs of a new clot, and the exam showed reduced lumbar flexion with bilateral sacroiliac tenderness, CRP 24, and sacroiliitis on X-ray. The clinician diagnosed an ankylosing spondylitis flare, stopped naproxen, started acetaminophen, continued rivaroxaban 20 mg once a day and sulfasalazine 1000 mg twice a day, and arranged a rheumatology telehealth visit and a ride benefit.

note:
Doctor: Good to see you. I have you down as a 67-year-old male here for prediabetes and metabolic syndrome. How have things been since I saw you last?

Patient: Not great, honestly. I work nights at the warehouse and my schedule keeps changing. Some weeks it's four nights, some weeks it's six. I eat whenever I can, usually vending machine stuff around three in the morning, and I sleep maybe five hours in the daytime. I'm tired a lot.

Doctor: That's a hard schedule for blood sugar and weight. Any excessive thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision?

Patient: No, none of that.

Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath when you walk? Any numbness in your feet?

Patient: No chest pain, no shortness of breath, and no numbness.

Doctor: Good. Let's go through your medicines, starting with the metformin.

Patient: I'm supposed to take the extended-release 500 mg once a day, but honestly only about half the time. The copays add up with everything else, so I stretch my refills and skip some days.

Doctor: And the others?

Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg once a day. Atorvastatin, I take 80 mg at night before work. Hold on, the bottle says 40 mg. Yeah, 40 mg. I only take it a few days a week because it's the one my plan charges the most for. Omeprazole 20 mg every morning when I get home, and the baby aspirin, 81 mg every day.

Doctor: So atorvastatin 40 mg, taken a few days a week. Got it. Now your numbers. Blood pressure is 138/84, heart rate 76, weight 104 kilograms, BMI 33.5, and waist 112 centimeters. Heart sounds are regular, lungs are clear, there's no leg swelling, and your feet have normal sensation to monofilament testing with good pulses. Your labs from last week show an A1c of 6.2%, fasting glucose 118, triglycerides 210, HDL 36, LDL 112, creatinine 1.0, and eGFR 78.

Patient: Is that bad? Am I going to get diabetes?

Doctor: You're at real risk, but this is the stage where we can change the course. My impression is prediabetes and metabolic syndrome, with obesity, hyperlipidemia, high blood pressure, and GERD. Here is the plan. First, I'm increasing your metformin extended-release from 500 mg to 1000 mg once a day, taken with your first real meal after you wake up, whatever shift you worked. That way the timing stays the same even when your schedule changes.

Patient: What about the cost? I can't keep skipping, but I can't afford more.

Doctor: Understood. Metformin is among the cheapest drugs we have, and our pharmacist will move all your prescriptions to a 90-day supply on the lowest-cost generic list so your copays drop. Please take atorvastatin 40 mg every day, not just a few days a week. Continue lisinopril 20 mg once a day and omeprazole 20 mg every morning. I'm stopping the aspirin 81 mg, because you've never had a heart attack or stroke and at your age the bleeding risk outweighs the benefit.

Patient: Okay. What about eating? I can't exactly cook at 3 a.m.

Doctor: I'm referring you to a dietitian who works with night-shift workers, to plan meals you can pack and eat at set times. Try ten-minute walks on your breaks, and keep your sleep as regular as you can. We'll repeat the A1c and a lipid panel in three months, and I'll see you back then. Call sooner if you get very thirsty or urinate a lot.

Patient: That sounds doable. Thank you.
summary: A 67-year-old male night-shift warehouse worker with an irregular schedule presented for prediabetes and metabolic syndrome, reporting fatigue and cost-related skipping of metformin and atorvastatin, with no excessive thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, chest pain, shortness of breath, or numbness. He first said he takes atorvastatin 80 mg but corrected this to 40 mg after checking the bottle. Blood pressure was 138/84, A1c 6.2%, triglycerides 210, and LDL 112. The clinician diagnosed prediabetes and metabolic syndrome with obesity, hyperlipidemia, high blood pressure, and GERD, increased metformin extended-release to 1000 mg once a day, stopped aspirin, and continued the other medicines. A pharmacist cost review, a night-shift dietitian referral, and repeat A1c and lipid panel in three months were planned.

The patient is an 8-year-old male seen in pediatric clinic with his mother for follow-up of ADHD, combined presentation, diagnosed four months ago. He started methylphenidate extended-release 18 mg every morning six weeks ago. His mother reports clear improvement in morning focus: he finishes his homework with fewer reminders, and his teacher notes better attention during reading and math. However, the medication seems to wear off by late afternoon, when he becomes restless again and has trouble completing homework. He has decreased appetite at lunch but eats well at breakfast and dinner. He also has trouble falling asleep, usually about an hour after bedtime. His mother denies headaches, stomachaches, tics, mood swings, palpitations, and chest pain. He takes cetirizine 5 mg daily for seasonal allergies and no other medications.

On examination, blood pressure is 98/62 and heart rate 88. Weight is 24.6 kg, down from 25.4 kg at the last visit, and height is 129 cm. Heart rhythm is regular without a murmur, lungs are clear, and no tics are observed. The Vanderbilt teacher rating scale shows 5 of 9 inattention items positive, improved from 8 of 9 at baseline. Vision and hearing screening were normal today.

My assessment is ADHD, combined presentation, with a partial response and afternoon wear-off. He has mild weight loss from decreased appetite on the stimulant, and sleep-onset insomnia that is probably related to the late-day effect of the medication and to bedtime routine. His seasonal allergies are stable.

For the plan, I am increasing methylphenidate extended-release from 18 mg to 27 mg every morning, to be given before school. We discussed giving a high-calorie breakfast before the dose and a substantial snack after school, and serving dinner later in the evening. I am starting melatonin 1 mg 30 minutes before bedtime with a consistent bedtime routine and no screens in the hour before sleep. Continue cetirizine 5 mg daily. If his weight falls again at the next visit, we will reconsider the dose. His mother will ask the teacher to complete another Vanderbilt rating scale, and we will recheck blood pressure, heart rate, and weight at a return visit in four weeks.

Doctor: Hi, I'm the provider here in urgent care. I see you're a 27-year-old female here because of bleeding. Tell me what's going on.

Patient: My period has been going on for about twelve days now. It started out normal, but then I had really heavy bleeding, and for a few days I was soaking through a pad every two hours. It's lighter today, but I'm still passing small clots.

Doctor: Are your periods usually irregular?

Patient: Pretty irregular for the past year. Sometimes they're six weeks apart, sometimes closer.

Doctor: Is there any chance you could be pregnant?

Patient: I mostly use condoms. I took a home test last week and it was negative.

Doctor: Any lightheadedness, fainting, or racing heart?

Patient: I felt a little lightheaded yesterday when I stood up fast, but no fainting and no racing heart.

Doctor: Any belly pain, fever, or unusual discharge?

Patient: No belly pain, no fever, and no discharge or bad smell.

Doctor: Any easy bruising or nosebleeds? And are you taking any medicines?

Patient: No bruising and no nosebleeds. I just take a multivitamin sometimes.

Doctor: Okay. Let me share what I found. Your blood pressure is 112/70, heart rate 92, temperature 98.6, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Your abdomen is soft and not tender. On the pelvic exam there is a moderate amount of blood in the vagina, your cervix looks normal and is closed, and there is no cervical motion tenderness. Your urine pregnancy test today is negative. Your complete blood count shows a hemoglobin of 10.2, which is a little low from the blood loss.

Patient: So what is going on? Is it serious?

Doctor: My impression is abnormal uterine bleeding, most likely from irregular ovulation, with mild anemia. Nothing here looks like an emergency. For the plan, I'm starting medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg once a day for 10 days to stop the bleeding. You will probably have a period-like bleed a few days after you finish. I'm also starting ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food for 5 days to reduce the flow, and ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day for the low blood count. I'm ordering a TSH and a pelvic ultrasound, which you can get this week, and I want you to see a gynecologist within one to two weeks.

Patient: What if the bleeding gets heavy again?

Doctor: Go to the emergency room if you soak more than one pad an hour for two hours in a row, feel faint, or have severe pain.

Patient: Okay, thank you.

She felt lightheaded once on standing but denied fainting, racing heart, belly pain, fever, discharge, bruising, and nosebleeds. Vitals were stable, the abdomen was soft, the pelvic exam showed blood in the vagina with a closed normal cervix, the urine pregnancy test was negative, and hemoglobin was 10.2. The clinician diagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding, most likely from irregular ovulation, with mild anemia. Medroxyprogesterone acetate, ibuprofen, and ferrous sulfate were started, with TSH, pelvic ultrasound, and gynecology follow-up arranged.

Rheumatology progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is a 46-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus who was admitted three days ago with a flare causing inflammatory polyarthritis of the hands and knees, fatigue, and new foamy urine with ankle swelling. There were no events overnight. His joint pain and morning stiffness are improving. He denies fever, chest pain, new rash, oral ulcers, and headache.

Current inpatient medications are methylprednisolone 500 mg IV daily, with today being the third and final dose, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily continued from home, and lisinopril 10 mg daily, which was started on admission for blood pressure and proteinuria.

Vital signs this morning: blood pressure 146/90, heart rate 82, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.3 F, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam he has mild bilateral ankle edema and less swelling over the metacarpophalangeal joints than on admission. There is no rash and no oral ulcers, and his heart and lungs are clear.

Labs show creatinine 1.1, stable from 1.2 on admission, hemoglobin 11.4, and platelets 168. The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 1.8 g/g. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein with red blood cells and a few red cell casts. Anti-dsDNA is elevated at 240 IU/mL, C3 is low at 52, and C4 is low at 8.

My assessment is a systemic lupus erythematosus flare with inflammatory polyarthritis and probable lupus nephritis, responding to pulse steroids. His hypertension is above goal.

For the plan, complete the last methylprednisolone dose today and start prednisone 60 mg daily tomorrow morning. Continue hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and continue lisinopril 10 mg daily, with a repeat creatinine and potassium in two days. Nephrology will perform a renal biopsy tomorrow, and we will decide on additional immunosuppression after the pathology result. Monitor blood pressure and daily weights. Anticipate discharge in several days if his renal function remains stable.

note:
Pulmonology progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is a 25-year-old female admitted with acute pulmonary embolism, diagnosed on CT pulmonary angiogram that showed bilateral segmental emboli, after five days of shortness of breath and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. A left leg venous duplex showed a popliteal deep vein thrombosis. She had been taking a combined oral contraceptive for two years, which is the likely provoking factor, and she has no other risk factors. She has a documented allergy to ibuprofen and other NSAIDs, which cause hives and lip swelling, so these are avoided.

Overnight there were no events. Her pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath are both improving, and she walked in the hallway this morning without a drop in oxygen saturation. She denies hemoptysis, syncope, palpitations, fever, and any bleeding. She has been on a heparin infusion since admission, and the combined oral contraceptive was stopped on admission. She needed acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pleuritic pain, about twice yesterday.

Vital signs this morning: heart rate 88, down from 112 on admission, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 18, temperature 98.6 F, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air, compared with 91% on admission. Her lungs are clear and her heart rhythm is regular without a murmur. There is mild left calf swelling and tenderness, unchanged. The echocardiogram shows normal right ventricular size and function, and troponin was negative. Hemoglobin is 12.8, platelet count 245, and creatinine 0.7. A urine pregnancy test was negative.

My assessment is acute bilateral pulmonary embolism with left popliteal deep vein thrombosis, hemodynamically stable and low risk, provoked by an estrogen-containing contraceptive, and clinically improving.

For the plan, stop the heparin infusion and start apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, for at least three months of treatment. Continue acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pleuritic pain, and avoid NSAIDs because of her allergy and the bleeding risk on anticoagulation. She should not take estrogen-containing contraception again, and gynecology will counsel her on non-estrogen options. We reviewed bleeding precautions and when to seek care. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if she remains stable on room air, with outpatient hematology follow-up and pulmonary clinic follow-up in six weeks.

She denied hemoptysis, syncope, palpitations, fever, and bleeding, and she has a documented allergy to ibuprofen and other NSAIDs. Heart rate had fallen to 88, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and the echocardiogram and troponin were reassuring. The heparin infusion was stopped and apixaban 10 mg twice daily was started, followed by 5 mg twice daily, with acetaminophen for pain, NSAIDs avoided, and the contraceptive permanently stopped. Discharge is anticipated tomorrow with hematology and pulmonary follow-up.

Neurology progress note, hospital day 4. The patient is a 60-year-old female admitted four days ago after a neighbor found her confused at home. She lives alone, her only family is a sister in another state, and she has limited social support. The history is of progressive memory loss and confusion, word-finding difficulty, missed medications, unpaid bills, and spoiled food in her refrigerator. When first interviewed she said the problems began about six months ago, but her sister, reached by telephone, clarified that the changes have been present for about two years and have worsened over the last six months. She also first reported taking sertraline 100 mg daily, but her pillbox and pharmacy fill history confirm sertraline 50 mg daily.

Past history includes hypothyroidism, hypertension, T2DM, depression, and overactive bladder. Home medications are levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, which she takes irregularly, lisinopril 10 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, and oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for urinary urgency. She denies headache, fever, focal weakness, seizures, hallucinations, and falls. She does not drink alcohol.

Overnight there were no events, and she has been calm and cooperative. She is oriented to person and place but not to the date. The CAM was negative, so delirium is not present. Vital signs: blood pressure 138/80, heart rate 74, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.2 F, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam she is alert and pleasant, cranial nerves are intact, there is no focal weakness or parkinsonism, reflexes are symmetric, and her gait is mildly slow. MoCA is 19 out of 30, with deficits in delayed recall, orientation, naming, and executive tasks.

Data review: CT head on admission showed no acute findings. MRI brain shows moderate generalized cerebral atrophy with chronic small vessel ischemic changes and no acute infarct or mass. Labs show sodium 138, creatinine 0.9, glucose 128, A1c 7.4%, TSH 9.8, and vitamin B12 level 245 pg/mL, which is borderline low. Folate is normal, RPR is nonreactive, and urinalysis is negative for infection.

My assessment is cognitive impairment, most likely multifactorial: a probable neurodegenerative process with a vascular contribution, worsened by undertreated hypothyroidism, borderline low B12, and the anticholinergic effect of oxybutynin. It is not currently safe for her to live alone without services.

For the plan, discontinue oxybutynin and manage urgency with timed voiding. Increase levothyroxine from 75 mcg to 100 mcg daily and repeat the TSH in six weeks. Start vitamin B12 1000 mcg daily and send a methylmalonic acid level. Continue sertraline 50 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. I am deferring a cholinesterase inhibitor until the reversible contributors are treated and she is reassessed in memory clinic. Physical and occupational therapy will assess function, including medication management. Social work will arrange a capacity evaluation for discharge planning, home health, meal delivery, and a pill dispenser, and will contact her sister with her permission. Discharge to short-term rehabilitation is anticipated. She should not drive. Memory clinic follow-up in four to six weeks, with formal neuropsychological testing as an outpatient.
summary: A 60-year-old female who lives alone with limited social support was admitted after a neighbor found her confused, with progressive memory loss, word-finding difficulty, and missed medications. Her sister clarified that symptoms have lasted about two years, and the pillbox confirmed sertraline 50 mg daily rather than the 100 mg she first reported. MoCA was 19 out of 30, CAM was negative, MRI showed moderate atrophy with small vessel changes, TSH was 9.8, and vitamin B12 was borderline low. The assessment was multifactorial cognitive impairment worsened by undertreated hypothyroidism, low B12, and oxybutynin. Oxybutynin was discontinued, levothyroxine was increased to 100 mcg daily, vitamin B12 was started, and social work, therapy, and memory clinic follow-up were arranged.
